issues.legal_issue: A conviction based wholly on circumstantial evidence cannot stand unless the established circumstances form a complete chain consistent only with guilt and exclude reasonable hypotheses of innocence.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence; the witness it principally relied on did not see the assault or the accused at the scene when he returned after hearing a cry.
That witness’s account that he turned back after travelling only a short distance but saw neither the accused nor the person who had cried was difficult to accept.
The complainant’s testimony denied witnessing the assault, contrary to the account in her complaint, and she said she had learned of the injury from other people.
A witness who was said to have helped move the injured person was not called to testify.
Although an axe bearing blood of the deceased’s group was recovered, the other evidence left a gap in the chain linking the accused to the assault.
issues.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence did not establish a complete chain pointing only to guilt. The conviction and sentence were set aside, and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hanumant Govind Nargundkar v. State of Madhya Pradesh, M.G. Agarwal v. State of Maharashtra, Pawan Kumar v. State of Haryana, State of U.P. v. Ashok Kumar Srivastava, Balwinder Singh v. State of Punjab, and Sudama Pandey v. State of Bihar, the circumstances must be fully established and must be conclusive, consistent only with guilt, and sufficient to exclude reasonable hypotheses of innocence. A complete chain is required; strong suspicion is insufficient, and where the proved circumstances reasonably support an inference in favour of the accused, the benefit of doubt applies.

predicates.criminal_conviction_based_on_circumstant: The prosecution sought and obtained a criminal conviction on evidence that did not directly establish the accused committed the act.
predicates.chain_has_material_gap: The circumstances relied on by the prosecution left an unfilled gap in linking the accused to the offence.
predicates.evidence_supports_reasonable_innocent_in: The proved evidence reasonably allowed an inference consistent with the accused’s innocence.

issues.definition: When a criminal conviction rests on circumstantial evidence and the chain has a material gap or the evidence supports a reasonable inference of innocence, the conviction must be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s evidence is not wholly rejected merely because the witness is declared hostile, but any portion relied upon must be closely scrutinised and may be accepted if consistent with the prosecution or defence.
material_facts: The complainant was declared hostile after her testimony contradicted the account in her complaint, although she admitted her thumb impression on the complaint.

Her testimony denied witnessing the assault and described learning of the injury from other people, while portions of her account were consistent with what happened after the injured person was found.
issues.conclusion: Declaring the complainant hostile did not automatically exclude her evidence; a consistent portion could be accepted only after close scrutiny. Her testimony, considered in this case, did not support the prosecution’s account of the assault.
issues.legal_principle: State of U.P. v. Ramesh Prasad Misra & Anr. holds that the evidence of a hostile witness is not to be totally rejected if it favours either side; it may be subjected to close scrutiny, and the portion consistent with the prosecution or defence may be accepted.

predicates.criminal_evidence_case: The evidence was considered in a criminal proceeding.
predicates.witness_declared_hostile: A witness was treated as hostile after giving testimony inconsistent with an earlier account.
predicates.testimony_contains_portion_consistent_wi: Some part of the witness’s testimony accords with the case advanced by the prosecution or the defence.

issues.definition: In a criminal proceeding, if a witness is declared hostile and some testimony accords with a party’s case, that portion may be accepted after close scrutiny.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may examine the evidence in detail when a lower court’s failure to assess it properly may prejudice the accused and cause a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The trial court relied strongly on the principal witness and convicted the accused, and the High Court affirmed the conviction.
The courts below did not address the significance of the witness’s account, the contradictory testimony of the complainant, or the absence of a material witness.
The Supreme Court found that the failure to address these matters went to the root of the case and caused a miscarriage of justice.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court examined the evidence in detail and intervened because the lower courts’ treatment of it risked prejudice and resulted in a miscarriage of justice.
issues.legal_principle: Although the Supreme Court ordinarily does not undertake an analysis or appreciation of evidence, a justice-oriented approach permits it to examine the evidence where it finds a lacuna in the High Court’s assessment that may prejudice the accused and result in a miscarriage of justice.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The matter before the court is an appeal in a criminal case.
predicates.lower_court_evidence_assessment_has_mate: A lower court failed to address a significant feature of the evidence when assessing the case.
predicates.accused_may_suffer_prejudice_or_miscarri: The failure to assess the evidence may prejudice the accused or result in a miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, when a material lacuna in the lower court’s evidence assessment may prejudice the accused or cause a miscarriage of justice, the appellate court may re-examine the evidence.
